title: The Storming of the Bastille
subject: histoire
description: On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed a fortress that held only **7 prisoners**. That act became the symbol of the French Revolution.

hero.hook: On July 14, 1789, Paris storms a fortress... for gunpowder.

blocks.text: On **July 14, 1789**, a crowd of Parisians marched on the **Bastille**, an old fortress on the eastern edge of Paris. They had not come to free thousands of prisoners. What they wanted above all was **gunpowder** to defend themselves.
That day King **Louis XVI** watched his own capital slip away from him. A riot over weapons became the founding act of the **French Revolution**. Here is how it happened.

sections.title: France on the edge of bankruptcy

blocks.text: By 1789 the kingdom was ruined. Helping the American colonies during the [[American Revolutionary War]] had cost an enormous amount. To raise new taxes, Louis XVI summoned the **Estates General** in May: an assembly of the clergy, the nobility, and everybody else.

blocks.caption: The Estates General of 1789: the Third Estate facing the clergy and the nobility

blocks.text: Under the [[Ancien Régime and the three estates]], society was cut into three. Clergy and nobility kept their privileges. The **Third Estate**, which was almost the entire population, had a single vote. Blocked, it declared itself the **National Assembly** on **June 17**. Three days later, at the **Tennis Court Oath**, the deputies swore not to separate until they had written a constitution.

The king seemed to give in, but he moved about **30,000 soldiers** into position around Paris. On **July 11**, he dismissed **Jacques Necker**, his very popular finance minister. Panic swept the capital.

On **July 12** and **13**, Paris rose up. Crowds burned the toll gates where taxes were collected at the city entrances. They looted the gunsmiths. On the morning of the **14th**, the crowd seized about **32,000 firearms** at the **Invalides**. Only the powder was missing.

blocks.caption: The storming of the Bastille, July 14, 1789

blocks.text: That day the Bastille held only **7 prisoners**: four forgers, two men judged insane, and one aristocrat. Its strength lay almost entirely in what it stood for.

Rumor said the powder was inside the Bastille. For many Parisians that prison embodied the king's arbitrary power, above all through the [[lettre de cachet]], an order of imprisonment without trial. The governor, **de Launay**, refused to open the gates. At about **1:30** in the afternoon, shots rang out: **98 dead** among the attackers. Soldiers who came over to the people's side brought up cannon. By late afternoon the fortress fell. De Launay was lynched in the street.

sections.title: When a revolt becomes a revolution

blocks.text: On **July 15**, Louis XVI was woken up. “Is this a revolt?” he asked. The answer came back: “No, Sire, it is a revolution.” A small irony of the calendar: in his hunting diary the king had written “Nothing” for the 14th.
**Palloy**, the contractor hired to demolish the Bastille, had dominoes carved from its stones and gave a set to the king's son, “so that he may play with the remains of despotism”.

The king called Necker back, pulled his troops out and accepted the **tricolor cockade**. In the countryside the news fed [[The Great Fear]]: peasants, afraid of noble revenge, burned the papers that recorded manorial dues. During the night of **August 4, 1789**, the Assembly abolished privilege.

sections.title: From July 14 to a national holiday

blocks.text: Demolition of the Bastille began the very next day. A year later, the **Festival of the Federation** celebrated national unity. But July 14 only became the national holiday in **1880**, under the Third Republic.

blocks.text: On **July 14, 1789**, Paris took the Bastille to get gunpowder. That act turned a financial crisis into a revolution and hastened the end of a society built on privilege.
